skill.name: azure-appconfiguration-ts
skill.description: Build TypeScript applications with Azure App Configuration, feature flags, dynamic refresh, Key Vault references, labels, and snapshots.
skill.summary: Use Azure App Configuration patterns in TypeScript services and applications.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: Static analysis mostly flagged Markdown code fences and TypeScript template literals as Ruby or shell backtick execution, which are false positives. The environment variable and URL examples are standard Azure SDK documentation patterns with placeholders and no evidence of exfiltration. One content-level concern remains because sample loops print configuration values that could expose secrets if copied into production.

remediation.issue: Configuration values are printed in sample loops.
remediation.suggestion: Show key names with redacted values, or warn readers not to log setting values or resolved Key Vault references.

remediation.issue: The connection string example includes a Secret placeholder.
remediation.suggestion: Prefer endpoint plus DefaultAzureCredential, and describe connection strings as a local fallback only.

semantic_findings.title: Configuration Values Printed to Logs
semantic_findings.description: The examples print each configuration key and value to console output. App Configuration can contain sensitive settings or resolved Key Vault references, so copied code could leak secrets to logs.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The examples explicitly log setting.value in list loops. The impact depends on the stored values, so this is a clear exposure pattern without evidence of malicious intent.

content.value_statement: Teams need consistent configuration across TypeScript services. This skill provides Azure App Configuration patterns for settings, feature flags, dynamic refresh, and Key Vault references.
actual_capabilities: Shows package choices for the Azure App Configuration SDK, provider, and feature management library.
Demonstrates client authentication with DefaultAzureCredential and connection strings.
Covers create, read, update, delete, lock, unlock, labels, and snapshots for settings.
Explains provider loading, dynamic refresh, Key Vault references, and object mapping.
Provides feature flag creation and evaluation examples with targeting context.
Lists SDK types and best practices for labels, snapshots, refresh, and RBAC.
limitations: Does not provision Azure resources or assign RBAC roles.
Does not validate current Azure SDK API changes or package versions.
Does not include production telemetry or deployment automation.
Examples need project-specific error handling and secret review.

use_cases.title: Centralize Service Configuration
use_cases.description: Move TypeScript service settings into Azure App Configuration with labels, prefixes, and provider loading.

use_cases.title: Add Feature Flags
use_cases.description: Create and evaluate feature flags with targeting groups and refresh behavior for gradual rollout.

use_cases.title: Prepare Release Snapshots
use_cases.description: Use snapshots and labels to preserve release configuration and recover archived versions.

prompt_templates.title: Choose Packages
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new TypeScript app.
prompt_templates.prompt: Show me which Azure App Configuration TypeScript packages to use for an Express app with feature flags.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Client
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me create an Azure App Configuration client in TypeScript using DefaultAzureCredential and environment-based endpoint configuration.

prompt_templates.title: Load Dynamic Settings
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a TypeScript provider setup that loads app settings by label, trims key prefixes, and refreshes configuration during requests.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Production Configuration
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a production Azure App Configuration strategy with labels, snapshots, Key Vault references, feature targeting, and safe logging guidance.

output_examples.input: I need to add feature flags to a Node.js API.
output_examples.output: A setup plan with packages, provider loading steps, feature manager usage, targeting rules, and refresh considerations.

output_examples.input: I need separate development and production settings.
output_examples.output: A label and key prefix strategy that separates environments while keeping common TypeScript access patterns.

output_examples.input: I need configuration refresh without restarting a service.
output_examples.output: A dynamic refresh approach with refresh intervals, middleware placement, and notes about non-blocking update behavior.

best_practices: Prefer DefaultAzureCredential and Azure RBAC when possible.
Use labels and key prefixes to separate apps and environments.
Avoid logging full setting values, especially connection strings and resolved secrets.
anti_patterns: Do not place real connection strings in prompts, docs, or screenshots.
Do not copy sample console logging into production observability.
Do not use broad key filters when a service needs only a small prefix.

faq.question: What does this skill help build?
faq.answer: It helps build TypeScript applications that use Azure App Configuration for settings, feature flags, refresh, labels, and snapshots.

faq.question: Does it require Azure credentials?
faq.answer: The examples assume an Azure App Configuration endpoint or connection string. Use managed identity and RBAC when possible.

faq.question: Can it help with feature flags?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers low-level feature flag creation and runtime evaluation through the Microsoft feature management library.

faq.question: Does it manage Azure resources for me?
faq.answer: No. It provides SDK usage patterns, but resource creation and role assignment remain outside the skill.

faq.question: Can it resolve Key Vault references?
faq.answer: Yes. It shows provider options for Key Vault references when the application has the required credentials and permissions.

faq.question: Is the content safe for production use?
faq.answer: Treat the examples as starting points. Add error handling, redaction, monitoring, and current package validation before production use.
